Senses.Note: The label is related by wording to the Baizhang wild-fox case (百丈野狐), but the corpus does not restrict it to citations of that case. Its verbs are openly corrective: "tear apart" (裂破), "sweep away" (掃), and "show off tricks" (逞甚伎倆). A verse placed under the Baizhang case says, "a whole troop carries on wild-fox Chan; over five hundred lives, one saying comes round" (修行一隊野狐禪，五百生來一語圓). The verse's own narrative language is retained as a recorded case allusion and not generalized beyond that witness.

ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Speakers use ‘wild-fox Chan’ as an adverse label for Chan they present as counterfeit, distorted, or merely clever. The phrase can allude to the Baizhang fox case, but its attested use also ranges beyond that case as a charge against other people’s teaching or performance.
EvidenceBody: It is an adverse label within the Chinese Chan record, applied to claims, verbal display, or conduct that Lia’an Qingyu, Ruibai Mingxue, Fangrong Tongxi, or another named speaker rejects as counterfeit or distorted Chan. Liao'an praises lines whose every sound "tears apart wild-fox Chan" (聲聲裂破野狐禪) and elsewhere says to "painstakingly sweep away wild-fox Chan" (痛掃野狐禪). Ruibai calls it "wild-fox Chan from various quarters" (諸方野狐禪) when criticizing attempts to define a lineage from Bodhidharma's reply to Emperor Wu, "really, no merit" (實無功德). Fangrong, after the cited participant shouts and then has no reply, asks, "what tricks is wild-fox Chan showing off?" (野狐禪逞甚伎倆).
